Governor.job: The governor signs or vetoes bills, proposes the state budget, and appoints executive officials. The governor enforces laws and maintains peace, and serves as commander in chief of Georgia's military forces, including the Georgia National Guard when they are under state authority.

Lt. Governor.job: The lieutenant governor is next in line if the governor cannot finish the term. Any other duties are set by state law. As president of the Senate, the lieutenant governor presides over debate in the Senate chamber.

Senate.job: The winner is one of 100 votes on federal law, spending, treaties, and judges. The term is six years. Senate committees gather information through investigations and hearings in order to recommend legislation, and they evaluate presidential nominees for executive and judicial posts.

Attorney General.job: The attorney general is the state's chief legal officer. Which cases the office files, and whether it prosecutes crimes, depends on that state's law. In Georgia, the office gives legal opinions that bind state agencies and prosecutes public-corruption cases involving dealings with the state.

Secretary Of State.job: The secretary of state runs the duties this state assigns that office. Those duties are not the same in every state. Georgia's secretary of state is responsible for administering elections, registering corporations, regulating charities and securities, and overseeing professional license holders.

rick jackson.role: Founder of Jackson Healthcare, running for governor.
rick jackson.bio: His letter says he built Jackson Healthcare, which operates in all 50 states, helps care for more than 20 million patients a year, and generates over $3 billion in annual revenue. He describes a childhood in public housing and five foster homes, raised by a mother struggling with alcoholism.
issues: He says he is running to cut the income tax, freeze property taxes, and lower costs so Georgia is the most affordable state.
He says he stepped in when China threatened the U.S. antibiotic supply, and that Governor Brian Kemp called him during COVID to help supply doctors and nurses.
He says he will also work to secure the state.

keisha lance bottoms.role: Former Atlanta mayor running for governor.
keisha lance bottoms.bio: She was Atlanta's 60th mayor and says she is the first mayor in the city's history to have served in all three branches of city government, as a judge, a city council member, and mayor. She says the city balanced four budgets without a property-tax increase, layoffs, or furloughs, and that reserves stood near $181 million at the end of her term.
issues: She says that as mayor she secured major investments in affordable housing and a historic pay raise for Atlanta's first responders.
She says she supported small businesses and became a national voice on civil-rights reforms.
She says the city balanced its budgets through a downturn without property-tax increases, layoffs, or furloughs.

greg dolezal.role: Business owner and author of several Georgia laws, running for lieutenant governor.
greg dolezal.bio: He says he has built companies and employed families in Georgia, and that this business record is the experience he would bring to the office. His campaign presents him as someone who writes bills rather than only giving speeches.
issues: He says he wrote the Riley Gaines Act to keep men out of women's sports and out of girls' locker rooms.
He says a law he authored stopped DEI mandates in public schools, and that his Georgia Promise Scholarship was a broad education change for parents.
He says he led an effort to hold Fani Willis accountable and is running because he believes public safety, livelihoods, and children's futures are at risk.

josh mclaurin.role: Georgia state senator and attorney running for lieutenant governor.
josh mclaurin.bio: He has been a state legislator for eight years, first in the State House and now in the State Senate, and he represents Senate District 14. He is a Yale-educated attorney and a University of Georgia graduate.
issues: He says he passed a bipartisan law that for the first time set statewide rules on the car-booting industry.
He says he secured the first $1 million in the state budget for research into therapies for veterans' post-traumatic stress.
He says he has fought efforts at the Capitol to advantage corporations and to target vulnerable people for political gain.

mike collins.role: Trucking businessman running for the U.S. Senate.
mike collins.bio: He says he used to haul freight and now wants to unseat Senator Jon Ossoff. His campaign describes him as someone who has worked for a living, created jobs, and passed what he calls America First legislation in Congress.
issues: He says Georgia needs a senator who has met tight schedules in the trucking industry, where he says you do not get paid if you do not deliver.
He says working-class Americans are the backbone of the campaign and of the country, and he asks voters to join that fight.

jon ossoff.role: U.S. senator from Georgia seeking another term.
jon ossoff.bio: His campaign calls him a legislative workhorse and an investigator of corruption and abuses of power. It says he is the only Democratic senator up for reelection in a state Donald Trump won.
issues: He says he has worked to cap insulin costs for seniors at $35 a month and to lower housing costs.
He says he has worked to upgrade health care for pregnant women, babies, and children, and to crack down on the online exploitation of children.

brian strickland.role: Georgia state senator, Senate Judiciary chairman, and practicing attorney.
brian strickland.bio: He was born and raised in Henry County, still lives in McDonough, and says he practices law there. He was first elected to the Georgia House in 2012 and to the state Senate in 2018.
issues: He says that as judiciary chairman he handles the state's laws on courts, crime, and criminal procedure.
He says he wrote the law that fixed long delays in competency hearings and has been a leading voice for mental-health reform.
He says he worked to stop foster children from being housed in state offices and supported stronger laws on gangs, counterfeit drugs, and human trafficking.

tanya miller.role: Trial attorney and chair of the Georgia House Democratic Caucus, running for attorney general.
tanya miller.bio: She says her career has run from the courtroom to the Capitol, including work as a prosecutor and as a civil rights attorney. She says the law should serve people rather than political interests.
issues: She says she will go after consumer fraud, including predatory lenders, scammers, and price gouging.
She says she will take on corporate negligence and monopolistic practices that hurt small businesses.
She says she will use her prosecution experience on public safety and will defend voting and privacy rights.

tim fleming.role: State representative, former deputy secretary of state, and former chief of staff to the governor.
tim fleming.bio: He says that as deputy secretary of state under Brian Kemp he managed a $30 million budget and about 250 employees. He later served as Governor Kemp's chief of staff, overseeing day-to-day agency operations and helping manage a budget he puts near $60 billion, and he now represents House District 114.
issues: He says elections should be secure, accessible, fair, and trusted, and he says he will protect voter ID and election transparency.
He says he reformed professional licensing so a new license could be issued in five days and renewals became automatic.
He says he will cut red tape for small businesses, improve customer service, and use technology so state government works for Georgians.

penny reynolds.role: Democratic nominee for secretary of state; the campaign identifies her as Judge Penny Brown Reynolds.
penny reynolds.bio: The campaign says she has spent her life working for justice and is running to protect the vote and make government work for people. It says she brings executive leadership and wants the office to guard fairness and opportunity.
issues: She says the office should protect the right to vote and run elections that are fair, secure, and accessible regardless of zip code, race, or income.
She says she would empower small business, modernize professional licenses, and safeguard seniors.
She says she would press government accountability and build systems that serve the public.

jim kingston.role: Insurance professional running for Congress in Georgia's 1st District.
jim kingston.bio: He calls himself a lifelong son of southeast Georgia, raised on faith, family, and service. He says his insurance career showed him how federal red tape holds back small towns, farms, and growing communities, and he describes himself as a Trump conservative.
issues: He says he will fight to lower taxes so families and small businesses keep more of what they earn, and he wants regular appropriations, balanced budgets, and agency accountability for spending.

On health programs, he supports work requirements for able-bodied Medicaid adults, says Medicaid should not cover people in the country illegally, and says he will protect Medicare while rooting out waste and giving seniors more control of their care.
He says he is running to defend President Trump, make the district more affordable, and back border enforcement.

amanda hollowell.role: Organizer and chief of campaigns at Color Of Change, running for Congress.
amanda hollowell.bio: She says her roots are in Georgia's 1st District, where she has served on the Savannah Black Heritage Festival Committee and local civic boards. She holds a B.A. in American Studies from the University of California, Berkeley, and she describes herself as a mom and as a full-time caregiver for her father, a veteran.
issues: She says she will fight to fund rural hospitals, expand mental health care, and protect Medicaid, and she supports national paid family and medical leave.
She wants apprenticeship programs, the right to organize, and federal investments that reach port and other workers, plus housing and wages that let people who work in the district live there.

She says she will push flood protection and preservation of the Okefenokee, restore voting access, defend LGBTQ+ rights and reproductive freedom, and treat gun violence as a public-health problem, including a ban on assault weapons.

matt day.role: Candidate for Congress in Georgia's 2nd District.
matt day.bio: His campaign points to work in glazing, construction, software, and real estate, and he describes himself as a timber man. He says he is on a mission for God and country to fight corruption, waste, and the size of government.
issues: His local list includes fathers who show up, ending generational poverty, farmers, teachers, manufacturing, white-collar jobs, rural health care, timber, ports, and pharmacists.
He also says he is working to save the Okefenokee Swamp and lists national priorities that include Social Security, Medicare, and the cost of living.
He says he is going to Washington to fight what he calls a woke liberal agenda and to defend Christianity and conservative freedoms.

sanford bishop.role: U.S. representative for Georgia's 2nd District, seeking another term.
sanford bishop.bio: He says he is in his sixteenth term and is the top Democrat on the Appropriations Subcommittee on Agriculture. A Morehouse College and Emory Law graduate, he served in the Georgia House and Senate before his election to Congress in 1992, and he enlisted in the Army in 1969.
issues: He says the district's farms, including its peanut crop, need disaster aid, market access, rural broadband, and a farm bill that supports food security and local food networks.
He supports the Affordable Care Act, more accessible care, and funding for veterans' medical care, and he highlights Fort Benning and Albany's Marine Corps Logistics Base.
He describes his goal as jobs, education, safe communities, a clean environment, energy independence, and a strong defense, pursued alongside a balanced budget.

brian jack.role: U.S. representative and former White House political director.
brian jack.bio: He says he is a sixth-generation Georgian raised in Fayette County, a Woodward Academy and Pepperdine graduate who worked at Peachtree City Hall and later for Ben Carson. He says he joined Donald Trump's 2016 campaign and served as White House political director through that administration.
issues: He calls the border the country's most pressing issue and says he will push to finish the border wall, fund ICE and the Border Patrol, deport people he calls criminal immigrants, and rewrite immigration law around working-class prosperity.
He says he will return to tax cuts and energy production he credits with an earlier economic boom, arguing that spending and energy policy have driven up gas and grocery prices.
His issues list also names stopping crime, ending what he calls the weaponization of justice, and leading on digital innovation.

maura keller.role: Retired Army officer and former VA health worker running for Congress.
maura keller.bio: She says she served 26 years in the Army, from enlisted military police to lieutenant colonel, received the General Douglas MacArthur Leadership Award, and later worked in health care at the Atlanta VA. Born in Massachusetts, she says she has lived in Georgia for more than 30 years and is running again after getting no help from her member of Congress for veteran patients.
issues: She supports a higher minimum wage, labor rights, affordable housing, Social Security that keeps up with inflation, and student-loan relief, and she says she would vote against funding a war with Iran.
She backs the Agricultural Right to Repair Act, farm safety nets, prescription-drug caps, restored Medicare subsidies, and easier VA care, including telehealth for rural veterans.
She also calls for stronger border enforcement alongside faster legal immigration, legal protections for LGBTQIA+ and BIPOC Americans, and infrastructure to handle storms, floods, and heat.

hank johnson jr..bio: His campaign says he is in his tenth term representing parts of DeKalb and Gwinnett counties, and it describes him as a legislator focused on delivering results for the district.
issues: He says he supports DACA, temporary protected status, refugees, and immigrants who come to build a better life for their children.

He says he has delivered more than $350 million in federal investment for district job creation since January 2009, including $98 million he says saved more than 1,000 teaching jobs in DeKalb, Rockdale, Newton, and Gwinnett counties.
He says he will oppose efforts to take away affordable health insurance and will stand with consumers seeking coverage.

nikema williams.bio: Her campaign calls her a longtime advocate for women and working families who has taken that work to Congress. She says she wants every person in the district to be able to live what she calls the promise of America.
issues: She says she is working to stop corporate and hedge-fund purchases of single-family homes, fund whole-home repairs for low- and middle-income owners, and help families pass a home down without a formal deed.

She wants research funding, especially on women's health, and support for faith and community groups that deliver care, citing institutions such as Morehouse School of Medicine, Emory, and the CDC in the district.
She also says she will keep fighting for affordable health care, equitable public-school funding, voting rights, and reproductive health care, which she calls a human right.

kevin martin.role: Corporate controller running for Congress in Georgia's 6th District.
kevin martin.bio: He says he has spent 30 years as a controller, the person who audits the books, and that he is a fifth-generation native of Cobb County who has lived in the district his whole life. He says voters should be in charge of the people they elect.
issues: On schools, he wants federal education money returned to Georgia without federal strings, and he wants student aid and career programs to cover shorter technical training.
On the budget, he says Congress should pass a budget through regular order, fund core obligations first, and make every other program justify another appropriation.

He also says law enforcement should be funded, federal law should focus on people who have done something, there should be no national gun registry, and defense spending should start from readiness and replenishment rather than the size of the check.

lucy mcbath.bio: She says the title that matters most is mom. After her son Jordan Davis was shot and killed in 2012, she left a 30-year career at Delta Air Lines, worked with Everytown for Gun Safety and Moms Demand Action, and then ran for the seat once held by Newt Gingrich.
issues: She highlights House passage of universal background checks and red-flag laws, and she says her work in Congress is aimed at laws that help children and families.
A two-time breast cancer survivor, she says communities need affordable care, including cancer screening, contraceptives, and family-planning services, and she opposed defunding Planned Parenthood.

She supports the Equality Act to bar LGBTQ discrimination in work, housing, and credit, and she points to federal infrastructure spending for safe water, high-speed internet, and a cleaner environment.

rich mccormick.role: U.S. representative, emergency physician, and former Marine pilot.
rich mccormick.bio: He says he was raised by a single mother, worked his way through school, flew helicopters as a Marine, earned his medical degree at Morehouse School of Medicine, and treated Georgia families in the emergency room. He says he left the ER to fight for those same families.
issues: He says Congress should be judged by whether costs come down, communities are more secure, and Washington works for the people it serves.
He says he is fighting inflationary spending, deficits, and debt, and he introduced the Incentivize Savings Act so federal agencies have a reason to save taxpayer money.
He says he has helped bring more than $319 million back to the district and introduced the Litigation Reimbursement Act to push accountability in the legal system.

tony kozycki.role: Former Navy combat aviator and attorney running for Congress.
tony kozycki.bio: Raised in LaGrange, he says he attended the U.S. Naval Academy, flew the F/A-18 Super Hornet, and completed three combat deployments. He says he is running because Rich McCormick stopped showing up for the 7th District.
issues: He says members of Congress should not trade individual stocks or hide behind omnibus bills nobody reads, and he lists a ban on congressional stock trading as a way to rebuild trust.
He points to child-care costs, families priced out of homeownership, and full-time work that no longer covers a household, and he says he has a plan to lower those costs.
He says he will fight to lower health costs, protect coverage, and hold the insurance industry accountable, arguing that premiums were allowed to double.

austin scott.bio: He lives in Tifton and says his experience runs from the cattle farm to the boardroom. A University of Georgia graduate, he says he spent 20 years running his own small business and serves on the Intelligence, Armed Services, and Agriculture committees.
issues: He says he represents Georgia values and free-market principles, and that the goal is to protect personal freedoms, individual liberties, and economic opportunity for the next generation.
He says his agenda is to strengthen local businesses and benefit Georgia families.
He supports limited government, small-business job growth, a strong national defense, and a healthy agricultural economy.

andrew clyde.role: U.S. representative, Navy veteran, and firearms-business owner.
andrew clyde.bio: He says he was commissioned from Notre Dame, served 28 years in the Navy including three combat deployments to Kuwait and Iraq, then earned a master's from the University of Georgia and built Clyde Armory from a garage hobby into a company with two Georgia stores. Elected in 2020, he says he serves on the Appropriations and Budget committees.
issues: He says that on April 12, 2013, the IRS confiscated $940,000 from his business through civil asset forfeiture, and that the agency later offered to return part of it if he forfeited the rest.
He says most small-business owners hit by that process lacked the money to fight, and he presents the case as a fight against overreaching government.
On guns, he argues that taxes on firearms and ammunition, from the National Firearms Act to local per-gun taxes, treat a constitutional right as a privilege and could tax it out of reach.

houston gaines.role: Georgia state representative running for Congress.
houston gaines.bio: He says he was born and raised in Athens, where he still lives, and has served in the State House since 2019 for Barrow, Clarke, Jackson, and Oconee counties. He says his work has been helping small businesses grow, and that he now works with Carter Engineering in Oconee County.
issues: He says immigration enforcement should keep cooperating with ICE, deportations should continue, and the border should stay secured.
He says he led opposition to defunding the police in Georgia, backed hundreds of millions of dollars for law enforcement, and took on district attorneys he says endangered public safety.

He wants spending cuts and tax cuts to match what he calls Georgia's balanced budgets, more American manufacturing, a military rebuilt around strength, and a block on Chinese purchases of U.S. farmland.

john cowan.role: Neurosurgeon and small-business owner running for Congress.
john cowan.bio: He says his family has been in Bartow County since the 1930s, that he grew up on the family farm, graduated from Cartersville High School, and has cared for patients across the 11th District for decades. He and his wife, Dr. Anne Cowan, are raising four children, and he says he serves as a church elder.
issues: On health care, he says he would fix problems he attributes to the Affordable Care Act by lowering premiums, expanding choices, and putting patients in charge of their care.
He wants tax relief for families and small businesses, investment in American workers, and stronger domestic industry.
He supports proof of citizenship to vote, protections for speech, worship, and the right to bear arms, a ban on congressional stock trading, stronger ethics rules, and term limits.

ceretta smith.role: Grovetown council member, former Army medic, and union leader running for Congress.
ceretta smith.bio: She says she served nearly a decade as a U.S. Army medic, then spent twenty-five years in labor, civil, and human rights work as a federal employee and national union leader. She says that as a city council member she has championed children and held local government accountable.
issues: She says her vision for the 12th District is good jobs, strong schools, and healthy communities, with investment in new industries and infrastructure.
She says she will seek fair wages and health care now, and longer-term resources that keep the district thriving.
She says government should work for people rather than special interests, and that dignity, fair pay, and opportunity should not depend on ZIP code.

jasmine clark.role: Microbiologist and Georgia state representative running for Congress.
jasmine clark.bio: She says she has served in the Georgia House since 2018 after flipping a long-held Republican seat, and that she has been the legislature's leading science voice. She says she blocked a state school superintendent from banning AP African American Studies and challenged COVID data and an abortion-ban source she says was a fake medical organization.
issues: Her agenda lists lowering the cost of living, protecting education at every stage, and building an economy that works for people.
She also lists protecting rights and the most vulnerable, building safer communities, protecting democracy, and supporting veterans.
She says she is running because funding has been stripped from the CDC and the NIH and health care has been cut, and she says a policy that hits one group affects the whole community.

john salvesen.role: Candidate campaigning as Bongo for Georgia's 5th District.
john salvesen.bio: His campaign says he went undercover in what he calls a journalistic pursuit, did not like what he found, and concluded that neither party is giving people proper representation. He is running in Georgia's 5th District.
issues: He says that if elected he will own no stock, take contributions only from individuals, and report to constituents once a week on a podcast.
He says members disappear after they are elected, and he points to dropout rates and pockets of unemployment as a failure of representation.
He says he wants attention on what he calls poison in food, and he describes FedNow as a tracking program that would eliminate cash.

kelly esti.role: Navy veteran and small-business CFO running for Georgia's 8th District.
kelly esti.bio: His campaign says he served from 1999 to 2002 as a nuclear operator on the USS Henry M. Jackson, and that he was the first Black nuclear operator on that boat during his service. He earned a PhD in public policy from Walden University and is chief financial officer of BroTagz Embroidery. He says he served on the Hapeville zoning board, as a legislative aide to State Senator Donzella James, and on the effort that created the city of South Fulton.
issues: He says education is a public good and he would fund affordable learning beyond K-12, including job skills for the district's health-care, retail, and manufacturing workers.
He says he would strengthen Medicaid, Medicare, and VA care and fund rural clinics and hospitals, in a district he ties to Robins Air Force Base.
He says he would seek federal money for roads, broadband, and utility upgrades, including solar and wind where communities want them, and back labor standards for workers.

caitlyn gegen.role: Community organizer running for Georgia's 9th District.
caitlyn gegen.bio: Her campaign says she holds a bachelor's and a master's from the University of Georgia and a master's from the London School of Economics. She says she organized for women's rights and criminal justice reform, and that she helped unionize her workplace.
issues: She says she would fight for a livable minimum wage, more affordable housing, and Medicare for All so people in the 9th District can save and buy a home.
She says the wealthiest people, whom she calls the Epstein Class, are not paying their fair share of taxes, and that the revenue should fund social programs.
She says she would fund the Forest Service and protect the Roadless Rule, replace lead water pipes in rural North Georgia, and have Congress reclaim its war and taxation powers.

pamela delancy.role: Retired Army nurse colonel running for Georgia's 10th District.
pamela delancy.bio: Her campaign says she served 39 years in the Army, rising from enlisted soldier to colonel, including six years at the Pentagon on medical readiness for service members and their families. After retiring she survived gallbladder cancer and kept working as a registered nurse. She says McDonough and Henry County have been home for more than 20 years, and that she sits on the county's District 4 Board of Public Health.
issues: She says she would protect and expand health coverage for families, seniors, and veterans, including mental health care, and oppose cuts to benefits veterans have earned.
She says she would seek relief from housing and food costs, and that data-center growth should not come at the expense of the water supply.
She says she wants a secure border, an asylum process that works, a legal path to work that keeps families together, and oversight so enforcement follows the law.

chris harden.role: Attorney and small-business owner running for Georgia's 11th District.
chris harden.bio: His campaign says he grew up in a trailer park in Rossville, worked full time while going to school at night, and drove a forklift and loaded trucks before becoming an attorney. He says he is a husband and father of triplets, and that for more than fourteen years he has worked as a parent-defense attorney.
issues: He says he would make health care more affordable, expand Affordable Care Act premium tax credits, lower prescription costs, and improve access in rural communities.
He says he takes no corporate PAC money, would ban members of Congress and their immediate families from trading individual stocks, and would cut taxes for working and middle-class families.
He says data centers should not shift water and power costs onto ordinary customers, and he would invest in affordable energy and modernize the grid, roads, and bridges.

rick allen.bio: His office says he was elected in 2014. He founded the construction company R.W. Allen & Associates in Augusta at age 25, and he serves on the Energy and Commerce and Education and the Workforce committees. The son of a farmer, he says he spent eight years on the Agriculture Committee. He and his wife, Robin, live in Augusta.
issues: He says growing the economy is the way to create jobs, and that small businesses are being taxed and regulated while families face rising prices.
He says seniors paid into Medicare and Social Security and Congress should protect both, including Medicare Advantage, and lower seniors' health and prescription costs.
He says a four-year college is not the right path for every student, and he points to career and technical education, local control by parents and teachers, and school safety.

jim duffie.role: Navy veteran and businessman running for Congress in Georgia's 4th District.
jim duffie.bio: His campaign says he grew up with very little, served in the Navy's nuclear submarine force, and then built a business. He describes himself as a husband, father, grandfather, and great-grandfather, and not a career politician.
issues: He says he supports the FairTax Act, H.R. 25, which would end the federal income, payroll, estate, and gift taxes, abolish the IRS, and replace them with a national sales tax plus a monthly rebate so households at or below the poverty level pay no net federal tax.
He says families should be able to go to school, church, and the store without fear, and he would back law enforcement and first responders.
He says he would cut regulations that make it harder for small businesses to hire and grow, and defend the Second Amendment, religious liberty, and free speech.
